items.prompt: Read: its roots spreading across the path like the knuckles of a giant hand. What does this simile help the reader to picture?

options.text: a giant hiding behind the tree
options.why: This is a comparison. There is no real giant.

options.text: roots that are moving like fingers
options.why: The simile is about the shape of the roots, not movement.

options.text: a path made of stones
options.why: The simile describes the roots, not stones.

options.text: big, knobbly roots that stick up out of the ground

hints: Think about what knuckles look like.
A simile compares two things to help you picture one of them.
Ask: what shape would the roots be if they looked like knuckles?
items.explanation: Knuckles are the bumpy joints of your fingers. The simile helps us picture thick, lumpy roots rising out of the ground across the path.

items.prompt: Read: the years slipped through their fingers like sand. What does this simile suggest?

options.text: They spent many years playing on the beach.
options.why: The sand is part of a comparison, not a real beach.

options.text: Time passed quickly without them noticing, and they lost their chance to meet.
They were very careful with their time.
options.why: Sand slipping away suggests losing something, not being careful.

options.text: They kept the tin full of sand.
options.why: The tin held marbles, a hair clip and a photograph.

hints: Think about what happens when you try to hold sand in your hand.
The simile compares sand to the years.
Ask: did the friends keep their promise to dig up the tin together?
items.explanation: Sand runs through your fingers however hard you hold it. The simile suggests the years passed without the friends noticing, so they never met to dig up the tin.

items.prompt: Read: He turned his exile into an opportunity. What does this sentence tell you about him?

options.text: He made good use of a difficult situation.
He enjoyed being punished.
options.why: Exile was a punishment, but the sentence is about what he did with it.

options.text: He wanted to stay in the Netherlands for ever.
options.why: He returned home in 1919.

options.text: He did not care about Indonesia.
options.why: He returned to open schools for Indonesian children.

hints: Exile means being sent away from your country as a punishment.
An opportunity is a chance to do something useful.
Read the next two sentences. What did he do while he was away?
items.explanation: Instead of giving up, he used his time away to study education and earn a teaching certificate. This shows he made the best of a difficult situation.

items.prompt: Find and copy the two-word phrase that starts a paragraph. It shows the writer is about to weigh up both sides.
hints: Look at the first words of each paragraph.
The phrase comes just before the writer gives their own view.
Find the paragraph that contains I believe.
items.explanation: On balance tells the reader that the writer has weighed up both sides and is about to give a conclusion.

items.prompt: Which sentence from the text is a fact rather than an opinion?

options.text: I believe the benefits are greater than the problems.
options.why: I believe shows this is the writer’s opinion.

options.text: Most of the worries can be solved with careful planning.
options.why: This is what the writer thinks. It cannot be checked yet.

options.text: Many Indonesian cities, including Jakarta and Malang, already close some of their busiest roads to motor vehicles on Sunday mornings.
Supporters also argue that a car-free road brings a community together.
options.why: Argue tells us this is a view held by supporters, not a checked fact.

hints: A fact can be checked and proved true.
Opinions often use words such as I believe, argue or can be solved.
Ask of each sentence: could you check it in a newspaper or on a map?
items.explanation: You could check that cities such as Jakarta and Malang hold Car Free Days, so this is a fact. The other sentences give views.

items.prompt: The writer calls the monsoon the clock that sets the rhythm of the year. What does this metaphor suggest?

options.text: The monsoon is a machine that tells the time.
options.why: This takes the metaphor too literally.

options.text: The monsoon makes music.
options.why: Rhythm here means a regular pattern, not music.

options.text: The monsoon decides when important things happen each year, such as planting rice.
The monsoon arrives at exactly the same time every year.
options.why: The writer says some years are wetter or drier, so it is not exact.

hints: A metaphor describes one thing as if it were another.
Think about what a clock does in our daily lives.
Look back at the paragraph about how the monsoon affects daily life.
items.explanation: A clock tells people when to do things. The metaphor suggests that the monsoon sets the pattern of the year, such as when farmers plant rice.

items.prompt: The two poems show different feelings about rain. Sort these lines by the feeling they show.

items.text: Our cat sits sulking by the door,

hints: Find each line in the poems first.
Poem A welcomes the first rain. Poem B comes after months of rain.
Ask of each line: does it sound like a celebration or a complaint?
items.explanation: Lines from Poem A, such as the laughter and the singing gutters, celebrate the first rain. Lines from Poem B, such as soggy socks and a sulking cat, show the speaker is fed up.

items.prompt: The explanation about the seasons says the dry season brings weeks with little or no rain. Which lines from Poem A show the effects of this?

options.text: Tonight the gutters are singing.
options.why: This happens after the rain has come.

options.text: The paddy fields cracked like old plates, / the river shrank to a thin brown thread
began their loud, croaking applause
options.why: This shows the frogs welcoming the rain.

options.text: A cloud the colour of wet slate / rolled over the volcano
options.why: This shows the rain arriving.

hints: Look at the first stanza of Poem A.
Find lines that describe the land before the rain came.
Ask: what happens to fields and rivers with little or no rain?
items.explanation: Cracked fields and a shrunken river show what happens after weeks with little or no rain. Both texts describe the dry season, one with facts and one with images.

items.prompt: Why does the speaker in Poem B mention August in the last stanza?

options.text: because August is the speaker’s birthday
options.why: The poem does not mention a birthday.

options.text: to explain that it also rains in August
options.why: The poem says the fields were dust in August, so it was dry.

options.text: to show the speaker has always hated rain
options.why: In August, the speaker begged for rain.

options.text: to show a funny change: in the dry season they wanted rain, and now they want the sun

hints: Think about the weather in August compared with February.
Read what the speaker begged for in August.
Compare that with what the speaker wants now.
items.explanation: In the dry month of August, the speaker begged for rain. Now, after months of rain, the speaker wants the sun. The change is funny because they got exactly what they asked for.

items.prompt: Ki Hajar Dewantara wanted children from ordinary families to have the chance to learn. Which detail in the report shows a similar aim?

options.text: The boat is painted bright blue and yellow.
options.why: This describes the boat, not its aim.

options.text: The boat brings library books to children who live far from any bookshop.
The boat stays in the harbour when the sea is rough.
options.why: This is a challenge, not an aim.

options.text: Books are kept in sealed plastic boxes.
options.why: This is about protecting the books.

hints: Think about what both Ki Hajar Dewantara and Pak Haris wanted for children.
Look for a detail about who the boat helps.
Ask: which children would not have books without the boat?
items.explanation: Both Ki Hajar Dewantara and the Pustaka Laut team wanted to give learning chances to children who would otherwise miss out.

items.prompt: Read: Sticky tape had lasted ten minutes of practice before peeling away like a banana skin. What does this simile suggest about the tape?

options.text: It was the same yellow colour as a banana.
options.why: The simile is about how the tape came away, not its colour.

options.text: It came off easily and could not hold the glove together.
It was stuck on much too tightly.
options.why: Peeling away means it came off, not that it stuck.

options.text: It smelt of fruit.
options.why: The comparison is about the action of peeling.

hints: A simile compares two things using like or as.
Think about how easily a banana skin peels away.
Ask: did the tape stay on or come off?
items.explanation: A banana skin peels off easily. The simile shows that the tape quickly came away and could not mend the glove.

items.prompt: The writer says the turtle’s magnetic signature is “rather like an invisible address”. Why does the writer use this comparison?

options.text: To explain an unfamiliar idea using something the reader knows.
To say that turtles can read house numbers.
options.why: The comparison is only to explain an idea, not a real address.

options.text: To suggest the writer is not sure the idea is true.
options.why: The phrase One idea is that already shows the uncertainty. The comparison is for clarity.

options.text: To make the text funny.
options.why: The tone is informative, not comic.

hints: Think about what an address does for a person.
The writer compares a hard idea with an easy one.
Ask: does a comparison like this make the idea easier to picture?
items.explanation: An address tells you where a place is. Comparing the magnetic signature to an invisible address helps the reader understand an unfamiliar scientific idea.

items.prompt: Which sentence from the letter best shows Yuki’s playful, joking tone?

options.text: The snowploughs rumble through the streets before dawn.
options.why: This describes something factual. It is not a joke.

options.text: Mum lays a mat inside the front door for our wet shoes.
options.why: This is a practical detail with no joking.

options.text: They say I am responsible for it.
In February our city holds a huge snow festival.
options.why: This is a plain fact.

hints: Look for a sentence where Yuki is teasing or laughing.
A playful tone often comes with a joke about someone.
Find the paragraph about her name.
items.explanation: Yuki jokes that her friends blame her for the snow because her name means snow. This is playful.

items.prompt: Sekar says her first line “wobbled like a worm”. What effect does this simile have?

options.text: It tells us there were worms in the workshop.
options.why: A simile is a comparison, not a real worm.

options.text: It shows she was angry with herself.
options.why: She says she stopped feeling embarrassed, so she was not angry.

options.text: It makes the diary honest and funny and shows how shaky the line was.
It shows she was good at drawing.
options.why: A wobbling line shows the opposite.

hints: Think about the shape of a worm.
A simile uses like or as to compare.
Ask: what does a wobbly worm tell you about her line?
items.explanation: The simile paints a picture of a shaky, curling line and gives the diary a light, honest tone.

items.prompt: The report mentions that half the seedlings from an earlier project died. What does this show about the way the report is written?

options.text: The reporter wants the project to stop.
options.why: The report also describes the care taken this time, so it does not oppose the project.

options.text: The reporter is giving a balanced view, not only praise.
The reporter wrote the report before the planting.
options.why: The report describes what happened, so it was written afterwards.

options.text: The reporter thinks the school is lying.
options.why: Nothing suggests this. The report says what the organisers did differently.

hints: Think about whether the report only says good things.
Balanced means showing more than one side.
Find the paragraph that begins Not everyone was sure.
items.explanation: By including villagers’ doubts and the earlier failure, the reporter shows both sides, which makes the report balanced and fair.

items.prompt: In “Pasar Malam” the poet writes “the night is wide awake”. What does this personification suggest?

options.text: Nobody at the market can sleep.
options.why: The poem is cheerful. It does not complain about the noise.

options.text: The night is a tired person.
options.why: Wide awake is the opposite of tired.

options.text: The market stays open all day.
options.why: The poem is about the night only.

options.text: The market at night feels full of life and energy.

hints: Personification gives human qualities to something that is not human.
Think about what a person who is wide awake is like.
Look at the other lines nearby: glows, moves, hum.
items.explanation: Giving the night the quality of being wide awake makes the market sound lively and full of energy.

items.prompt: How does the poet make the mood of “Pasar Pagi” different from “Pasar Malam”?

options.text: Pasar Pagi is frightening and Pasar Malam is calm.
options.why: Neither poem is frightening. Pasar Malam is lively, not calm.

options.text: Both poems show exactly the same mood.
options.why: The images and the pace differ.

options.text: Pasar Pagi shows purposeful work, while Pasar Malam shows play, light and fun.
Pasar Pagi is empty and Pasar Malam is crowded.
options.why: Pasar Pagi has trucks, aunties and sellers, so it is not empty.

hints: Compare the key images in each poem.
Lanterns and candy floss feel different from crates and tomatoes.
Ask: is each poem about playing or about working?
items.explanation: Pasar Malam uses glowing, playful images, while Pasar Pagi uses images of work such as crates, trucks and bargaining.

items.prompt: Mr Okafor says, “Every evening, when the sun goes down, I still look at the clock.” What does this suggest about how he feels now?

options.text: He is glad the job is over.
options.why: His tone is wistful, not relieved.

options.text: He is angry with the machines.
options.why: He states the change calmly and does not blame anyone.

options.text: He has forgotten about the lighthouse.
options.why: He still checks the clock at the same time.

options.text: He misses his work but says so quietly, without stating it directly.

hints: Think about what he does, not only what he says.
Old habits stay with you suggests a connection to the past.
Ask: would someone who had forgotten the job still watch the clock?
items.explanation: He never says I miss it, but his small habit shows that the work still matters to him. The writer lets the action show the feeling.

items.prompt: In the third paragraph, what does “astonishingly” mean in “astonishingly strong”?

options.text: in an amazing, surprising way
dangerously
options.why: Nothing suggests danger here.

options.text: slowly
options.why: Slowly does not describe how strong something is.

options.text: slightly
options.why: Slightly would make the sentence weaker. The writer is impressed.

hints: Look at the other words near it, such as light and strong.
The writer is trying to impress the reader.
Replace the word with each choice and see which makes sense.
items.explanation: Astonishingly means in a way that amazes you. It shows how impressed the writer is.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes the writer’s viewpoint about bamboo?

options.text: Bamboo should replace every other material.
options.why: The last paragraph says it is not a magic answer.

options.text: Bamboo is useful and impressive, but should be used with care.
Bamboo is overrated and not worth using.
options.why: The writer praises bamboo throughout.

options.text: Bamboo is dangerous to grow near homes.
options.why: The text never says this.

hints: Think about the writer’s words in the opening and the final paragraph.
Look for the word Yet in the last paragraph.
Ask: does the writer only praise bamboo, or also give a warning?
items.explanation: The writer admires bamboo but ends with a careful, fair view that it must be used wisely.

items.prompt: Read: The old bus coughed and wheezed up the hill like a tired grandfather. What does this simile make you picture?

options.text: a slow, noisy bus struggling to climb
a bus carrying grandfathers
options.why: The simile is a comparison. There are no grandfathers.

options.text: a very fast new bus
options.why: Coughing and wheezing suggest an old, slow bus.

options.text: a bus parked at the bottom of the hill
options.why: The bus is moving up the hill.

hints: Think of how a tired old person climbs a hill.
Coughed and wheezed are sound words.
Ask: would a fast new bus cough and wheeze?
items.explanation: The simile makes the bus seem old, slow and noisy, as if it were out of breath.

items.prompt: Kofi was angry when he left the room. Which verb best fits the gap? Kofi ___ out of the room.

options.text: drifted
options.why: Drifting is gentle, not angry.

options.text: wandered
options.why: Wandering is slow and aimless.

options.text: stomped
tiptoed
options.why: Tiptoeing is quiet and careful, not angry.

hints: Think about how angry people move.
The verb shows the feeling without saying it.
Which verb would make a loud noise?
items.explanation: Stomped suggests heavy, loud steps and shows anger better than the other verbs.

items.prompt: Read: I am writing to complain, for the third time, that the bus to our village still does not run on time. This is simply not good enough. What is the tone?

options.text: playful
options.why: There is nothing playful or joking here.

options.text: puzzled
options.why: The writer is not confused. They are sure of the problem.

options.text: shy
options.why: The writer speaks firmly.

options.text: firm and annoyed

hints: Look at the words complain and not good enough.
The phrase for the third time shows patience running out.
Imagine how a person would sound reading this aloud.
items.explanation: The writer has complained before and says it is not good enough, so the tone is firm and annoyed.

items.prompt: Read: Juicy Gold is the only drink champions choose. Every smart family already buys it. Which phrase puts pressure on the reader to agree?

options.text: Every smart family already buys it.
It comes in a bottle.
options.why: This is a neutral fact.

options.text: It is sold in shops.
options.why: This is a neutral fact.

options.text: Juicy Gold is a drink.
options.why: This is a plain statement that does not persuade.

hints: Persuasive texts often make you feel left out.
Look for a phrase that suggests clever people already agree.
Which choice is not just a plain fact?
items.explanation: Every smart family implies that anyone who does not buy it is not smart. This is a persuasive technique.

items.prompt: Read: The so-called festival was a noisy, muddy mess. The pathetic stage was tiny, and only a handful of bored people turned up. Choose all the words or phrases that show the writer’s negative opinion.

options.text: so-called
pathetic
festival
options.why: This is just a name for the event.

options.text: stage
options.why: This is a plain noun.

options.text: bored

hints: Opinion words show how the writer feels.
Plain nouns such as stage do not show opinion.
Look at the adjectives and the word so-called.
items.explanation: So-called, pathetic and bored all show the writer’s negative opinion. The nouns are neutral.

items.prompt: Sort each sentence into Fact or Opinion.

items.text: Jakarta is the capital of Indonesia.

hints: A fact can be checked and proved.
An opinion shows what someone thinks or feels.
Look for words such as tastiest, boring and better.
items.explanation: Facts can be checked. Words such as tastiest, boring and better show feelings, so they are opinions.

items.prompt: Read: Silent snow settled softly on the sleeping street. Which sound is repeated, and what effect does it create?

options.text: the p sound, creating a popping noise
options.why: There is no repeated p sound.

options.text: the g sound, creating a growling effect
options.why: There is no g sound in the line.

options.text: the s sound, creating a soft, hushing feel
the t sound, creating a sharp click
options.why: Only the s sound is repeated across the line.

hints: Say the sentence aloud and listen.
Alliteration repeats a sound.
Look at the first letters of silent, snow, settled, softly, sleeping and street.
items.explanation: The repeated s sound is soft and hushing, like falling snow.

items.prompt: Read: The wind whispered through the bamboo. What do we call it when a writer gives a human action to something that is not human? Answer with one word.
hints: The wind cannot really whisper.
The word begins with person.
Think of the device you used for the night being wide awake.
items.explanation: This device is personification. The wind is given the human action of whispering.

items.prompt: Text A: The new mall brings jobs, brighter streets and a cinema for local families. Text B: The new mall has swallowed the old market, and small traders are being pushed out. How do the texts differ?

options.text: They give different facts but both like the mall.
options.why: Text B is clearly critical of the mall.

options.text: Text A focuses on benefits and Text B on harm, so they present the mall differently.
Both say the mall is bad.
options.why: Text A is positive.

options.text: They are about two different places.
options.why: Both texts are about the new mall.

hints: Compare what each writer chooses to mention.
Look at verbs such as brings and swallowed.
Ask: is each text positive or negative about the mall?
items.explanation: Text A picks positive points and Text B uses strong negative words such as swallowed and pushed out.

items.prompt: Read: Bayu gobbled his noodles and wiped the bowl clean. The writer chose the verb gobbled to show that Bayu ate ___.
hints: Compare gobbled with ate.
Think about the sound of the word.
Wiping the bowl clean is another clue.
items.explanation: Gobbled suggests eating fast and hungrily.

items.prompt: Match each language device to an example.
pairs: The door slammed with a bang.
I have told you a million times.
hints: Think about what each device does.
A metaphor says something is something else.
Start with the sound word, bang.
items.explanation: Bang is a sound word, a million times is exaggeration, a question that needs no answer is rhetorical, calling a classroom a zoo is a metaphor, and repeating never is repetition.

items.prompt: Read: Of course the council asked the children for their ideas, then built a car park instead. Very helpful. What is the writer’s attitude?

options.text: sarcastic: the writer does not think the council was helpful
excited
options.why: There is no excitement. The writer is annoyed.

options.text: neutral reporting
options.why: The words Of course and Very helpful are not neutral.

options.text: grateful
options.why: Grateful people would not describe the council this way.

hints: Sarcasm says the opposite of what is meant.
Compare Very helpful with what the council really did.
Ask: did the council listen to the children?
items.explanation: The writer says very helpful, but the council ignored the children, so this is sarcasm.

items.prompt: Read: The wind howled like an angry wolf. Build a sentence that explains the effect of the simile.
items.answer: The simile makes the wind seem fierce.
hints: Think about the animal and its feeling.
Howled and angry give the mood.
Start with the subject, The simile.
items.explanation: Comparing the wind to an angry wolf makes it sound fierce and wild.

items.prompt: Poem A: The sea lay down like a sleeping cat, purring against the sand. Poem B: The sea rose up like a snarling beast, clawing at the rocks. How do the poems create different moods?

options.text: Poem A is about a cat and Poem B is about a beast.
options.why: Both poems are about the sea.

options.text: Only Poem A uses a simile.
options.why: Both poems use a simile with like.

options.text: Both poems make the sea sound equally calm.
options.why: Snarling and clawing are not calm.

options.text: Both compare the sea to an animal, but A uses gentle words and B uses harsh ones.

hints: Find the comparing words in each poem.
Look at sleeping and purring against snarling and clawing.
Ask: which poem feels safe and which feels threatening?
items.explanation: Both use similes about animals, but the gentle verbs in A and the harsh verbs in B create very different moods.

items.prompt: Read: The corridor was dark and silent. Something scraped behind the door, and a cold draught made the candle flicker. Choose all the phrases that create a tense mood.

options.text: The corridor
options.why: This names the place and creates no feeling on its own.

options.text: dark and silent
Something scraped behind the door
a cold draught made the candle flicker

hints: Tense words make you feel something might happen.
Mystery and darkness build tension.
Check which phrases are just a name of a place.
items.explanation: Darkness, a mysterious scrape and a flickering candle create a tense, spooky mood.

items.prompt: Read: “Isn’t it time we all did something about litter?” Why does the writer use a question?

options.text: To ask the reader to reply in writing
options.why: Writers do not expect a reply here.

options.text: Because the writer does not know the answer
options.why: The writer already has a view.

options.text: To give the reader instructions
options.why: A question does not tell you what to do.

options.text: To make the reader think and agree

hints: The writer does not need an answer.
It is called a rhetorical question.
Ask: what answer does the writer want you to give?
items.explanation: A rhetorical question makes the reader think and suggests the answer the writer wants.

items.prompt: Read: The council merely listened, then did nothing at all. Copy one word that shows the writer’s negative attitude to the council.
hints: Look for a word that makes listening sound not enough.
Look also at the end of the sentence.
Check the word after council.
items.explanation: Merely suggests that listening was not enough, and nothing at all is strongly negative.

items.prompt: A leaflet says: Our zoo has over 200 animals, a splash park and free parking. It does not mention the ticket price of Rp150.000. What might the reader suspect?

options.text: The leaflet shows only good points and leaves out something that might put people off.
The zoo is free.
options.why: If the zoo were free, the leaflet would likely say so.

options.text: The writer forgot to mention parking.
options.why: Parking is mentioned.

options.text: The price must be cheap.
options.why: The leaflet does not say this.

hints: Think about what the leaflet is trying to do.
Leaving things out can be a form of bias.
Ask: why would a leaflet skip the price?
items.explanation: A leaflet that lists only attractions and skips the price may be hiding information that would put readers off.
